title: The Christian King's Daughter and the Moslem

keywords: the christian king's daughter and the moslem
full_text:
In the maritime city of Genoa, a prosperous Muslim merchant of Alexandria named Mansur arrived with a cargo of Egyptian flax, Syrian damask, and pearls. While displaying his goods before the royal council, the King’s daughter, Princess Beatrice, was struck by Mansur’s dignified manners, absolute truthfulness in weights and measures, and gentle courtesy.

A sudden political coup forced the king into temporary exile, and the city was thrown into turmoil. Dishonest foreign traders seized their goods and fled, but Mansur remained, using his wealth to protect the king’s private treasury, sheltering the princess’s attendants, and managing the relief of the distressed citizens.

When the king returned to his capital with allied armies, he found his treasury intact, his daughter’s honor guarded with saintly reverence, and the city’s commerce preserved.

The king summoned Mansur and embraced him before all the nobles: 'You are of a different nation and faith, O merchant, yet your conduct has proved that honor and virtue speak a universal tongue.'

The king offered Mansur the governorship of the port and his daughter’s hand in marriage. Mansur, with noble modesty, declined the crown, choosing to remain an honest merchant, but established a permanent treaty of free trade and peaceful alliance between Genoa and Alexandria that endured for three generations, demonstrating that integrity builds bridges where armies can only dig trenches.
moral: Integrity in trade and unshakeable honesty in adversity command the respect of foreign courts.
